Similarly, Saudi Arabia and Qatar deploy sovereign capital into real estate, mining, and digital infrastructure. Gulf sovereign wealth funds, with patient capital and the capacity to move quickly on commercial timelines, are appealing partners. At a time when Chinese lending is dwindling in many places, Gulf states are filling the void. And many African governments prefer the Gulf model, in which investors tend to take equity in a project rather than saddling the borrowing state with debt.
This outside interest, however, does not mean that every African country can benefit from it. For African governments, the question is whether they can convert this new race for minerals into durable economic growth and material gains for ordinary people. Continental statistics obscure enormous variation. Over 80 percent of foreign direct investment in Africa is concentrated in just 15 countries, according to the United Nations.
Investors can tolerate many kinds of difficulties. They have less tolerance for uncertainty about whether contracts, regulations, or governments will remain stable long enough for an investment to pay off. Military governments that came to power in coups in Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger between 2020 and 2023 have drastically changed their countries’ economic landscapes and, worse, created enormous instability and hardship for local populations. Madagascar’s coup last year halted oversight of and reforms to the economy. In many jurisdictions, such as Egypt and Mozambique, sovereign debt distress or the risk of it leaves little fiscal room for other government spending.
A similar distinction applies to Africa’s urbanization and its demographic potential. Currently, big cities including Abidjan, Dar es Salaam, Johannesburg, Lagos, and Nairobi punch below their weight economically because they are cut off from one another by inefficient customs regimes, poor infrastructure, and incompatible payment systems. Population growth by itself cannot generate economic returns at a continental scale. And as the South African writer Jakkie Cilliers argued in these pages, Africa’s youth bulge will only be an asset if young people in the coming decades have access to education, formal employment, and functioning institutions. Otherwise, unemployed young people can become a source of instability. Governments across the continent, therefore, will diverge based on their ability to educate tomorrow’s workers and match their citizens with productive jobs. In sub-Saharan Africa, only 75 percent of people between the ages of 15 and 24 are literate, and much of the continent suffers from brain drain. There are, however, bright spots. Almost all children in Rwanda are enrolled in primary school.
Stable governance and trusted institutions separate those countries that can capitalize on oil, gas, or mineral deposits from those that suffer from resource curses. Zambia and its larger neighbor, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, both have vast mineral reserves. But Zambia’s systematic reforms since its 2020 debt default, such as changes to its tax structure, have helped restore stability and drawn in renewed investor interest, while the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with its continued conflict, presents much higher political and security risks.
In some parts of Africa, the obstacles to foreign investment are more acute. Since 2020, the continent has seen at least nine successful coups. Roughly 40 percent of the world’s conflicts are now in sub-Saharan Africa, especially in the Sahel and in Sudan, which is experiencing what may be the world’s worst ongoing humanitarian crisis. In places where the United States and France have withdrawn their forces, jihadist groups and Russian paramilitaries have moved to fill the vacuum. Even where there are stable governments, corruption and abuse remain endemic. In 2025, Freedom House documented a decline in political rights and civil liberties in 18 African countries, with improvement in just 11.
The questions investors ask in Africa are the same they ask everywhere else: Do governments protect property rights, enforce contracts, allow capital to move in and out, and invest in their people? Can businesses rely on basic infrastructure? Can goods move across borders efficiently? Do laws and regulations survive political change? How African governments answer these questions, rather than the existence of minerals or other potential advantages, will determine whether they can benefit from the current moment.
Among these constraints, perhaps none is more important than electricity. Nearly 600 million people in sub-Saharan Africa still lack access to electricity. No country in the modern era has industrialized without affordable, reliable power.
Africa possesses enormous energy resources, including offshore oil and gas fields along the coasts of Namibia and South Africa and copper—which is used in electric grids—in central Africa. Some governments have made remarkable progress in electrification. In 2009, just six percent of Rwandan households had electricity. By 2024, that figure had jumped to 75 percent, enabling Rwandans to start businesses, connect to the digital world, refrigerate goods, and keep schools running. Kenya and Uganda have made similar pushes.
Electrification will help unlock continental scale. Africa’s cities can grow rapidly but may not produce markets large enough to justify major investments if their factories lack reliable power to scale production and if barriers to trade—including the spoilage of goods—and undeveloped infrastructure continue to fragment consumer markets, supply chains, and capital. Something as simple as electricity that keeps more businesses and markets open at night can promote intra-African connections and commercial opportunities. To electrify their countries, governments will need to invest in power generation, transmission lines, and transformers.
Another way to overcome fragmentation and boost growth is to develop the African Continental Free Trade Area, a pact ratified by 50 of Africa’s countries aimed at creating one of the world’s biggest duty-free zones. Trade under its new terms is progressing, but governments still have a long way to go to implement it fully, including by harmonizing trade rules, tariffs, and customs procedures. Linking markets across African countries will be key to diversification, moving up the value chain, and generating long-term economic transformation.
There is unlikely to be a single African economic story. The same forces that are making the continent more important may also widen the differences among its countries and regions. But African leaders have a great deal of agency over which path their people take. The countries that open themselves up, to both intracontinental trade and outside money, are the ones that will likely fare best.
articles.summary: Who will benefit from the continent's investment boom?

articles.title: The New Red Sea Wars
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
ALAN BOSWELL is Project Director for the Horn of Africa at the International Crisis Group and host of The Horn, one of the organization’s podcasts.
On June 3, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told the U.S. Congress that the fighting that had raged for three years in Sudan was now a “proxy war” and blamed Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) for frustrating American efforts to bring the conflict to an end. Rubio was saying out loud what many observers already knew: what started as a domestic power struggle has morphed into a wider regional war, drawing in outside powers and spilling across Sudan’s borders.
The spread of the conflict in Sudan is part of a larger geopolitical transformation. For much of the past century, policymakers have treated the Horn of Africa and the Arabian Peninsula as separate strategic regions divided by the Red Sea. That distinction is now evaporating. Wars on one side of the sea increasingly alter the military calculations on the other. This entanglement is only deepening in the wake of the United States’ and Israel’s decision in February to launch a war on Iran, driving a deeper wedge between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh (which were already at odds), weakening the American-anchored security order in the region, and underscoring the importance of securing the Red Sea for shipping.
For the past decade, the UAE has been the most aggressive outside player in the Horn of Africa, establishing ports and military bases, offering large financial packages to key allies, and involving itself extensively in Sudan’s civil war. But the recent war in Iran, along with the breakdown of the Emirati-Saudi security partnership in Yemen last December, made Riyadh less confident of Washington’s protection, more anxious about the UAE’s security ties to Israel, and more intent on controlling the Red Sea’s security picture. And so as Saudi Arabia has leaned into an alignment with Egypt, Turkey, and Pakistan, it has also brought that alignment to bear to strengthen key partnerships in the Horn. It is trying to counter factions in the Horn that are backed by the UAE or Israel even as it struggles to manage threats from Iran and its allies—including the Houthis, who have seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
At the same time, the risk of conflict is increasing between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF), backed by Saudi Arabia and its allies, and Ethiopia, an ally of the emirates, as well as the chance that another direct war could erupt between Ethiopia and Eritrea. A new war between Ethiopia and Eritrea on the Red Sea would likely turn into a regional conflict that overlaps with the one in Sudan. And it would not only be aggravated by the existing Emirati-Saudi rift—it might well deepen that divide.
Some Middle Eastern governments once saw the Horn of Africa as a low-stakes theater in which they could compete for leverage at relatively little cost. But as wars in the Middle East and the Horn become inextricably linked, a single security sphere is coalescing. Unless leaders in both the Middle East and the Horn recognize how interconnected their security dilemmas have become, instability will continue to ricochet in both directions, and the overlapping conflicts and disputes will become harder to resolve.
In some respects, the growing entanglement between the Horn of Africa and the Middle East is a return to a historical norm. Over millennia, the sea connected present-day Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Yemen, and people, goods, and cultural trends moved regularly among them. Amharic, Ethiopia’s dominant language, and Tigrinya, widely spoken in Eritrea and northern Ethiopia, are both Semitic tongues. Christianity spread early to what is now northern Ethiopia, making it home to one of the world’s oldest Christian Orthodox traditions.
In the sixth century, an Aksumite ruler based in modern-day Ethiopia briefly conquered parts of Yemen. Not long afterward, the Prophet Muhammad sent some of his earliest followers across the Red Sea to take refuge with a Christian Aksumite king there. Islam later spread across the sea and along Africa’s Indian Ocean coast. From the sixteenth to the twentieth century, the Ottoman Empire ruled territory on both sides of the Red Sea, and Omani rulers built an empire tying the Arabian Peninsula to much of East Africa’s coastline, eventually moving their capital from Muscat to Zanzibar. These links persisted into the modern age. When the Saudi kingdom conquered the Hejaz region on the western Arabian Peninsula in the early twentieth century, elites in the port city of Jeddah sent their families across the Red Sea to Port Sudan for safety. And in April 2023, when war erupted in Khartoum, many Sudanese took refuge in Jeddah.
Starting in the twentieth century, however, a separation began to harden between the two sides of the Red Sea as European colonialism and nationalist movements severed governance links crisscrossing the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Connections remained—for instance, Persian Gulf wealth flowed to nearby African countries and African labor and exports flowed the other way after a 1970s oil boom transformed the Gulf economies, and Middle East countries played a substantial role in a war during that decade between Ethiopia and Somalia. But the political gulf between the Arabian and African Red Sea shores widened further after the end of the Cold War. The first Gulf War, in 1990-91, upended the Middle East and expanded the U.S. military footprint there, giving Gulf states a reprieve from managing their near abroad. Around the same time, polities in the Horn began to fragment. Somalia’s collapse drove Somaliland, a former British colony along the Gulf of Aden, to claim independence in 1991. Regime change in Ethiopia led to the 1993 secession of Eritrea, and an intensified civil war in Sudan eventually prompted South Sudan’s 2011 secession.
The United States made fraught and often counterproductive efforts to try to manage these convulsions in the Horn of Africa. Yet it rarely saw the Horn and the Middle East, or its role in each region, as linked. While Gulf states focused on threats emanating from Iran and the Levant, the Horn turned inward.
Regional leaders in these areas also did not view them as intimately connected. East African leaders such as Ethiopian President Meles Zenawi primarily sought influence across the African continent rather than across the Red Sea, championing institutions such as the African Union. Influential Christian elites in both Ethiopia and Kenya, the Horn region’s two strongest countries, have little attachment to the Arab world. Political power in the Persian Gulf region was concentrated in Riyadh and around the Persian Gulf capitals of Abu Dhabi and Doha, not the Red Sea shore. When Sudan partitioned, the process was led by the African Union with backing from the United States and Europe; the Arab world was on the sidelines.
During the turmoil of the Arab Spring, the Horn began to draw back into the Middle East’s sphere of influence. In a key turning point in 2011, Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdogan became the first non-African leader to visit Mogadishu, Somalia’s capital, in almost 20 years as he sought to expand Turkish influence in the region. The uprisings also destabilized Yemen and led to the Houthis’ takeover of much of the country in 2014. The decision by Saudi Arabia and the UAE to intervene militarily against the Houthis in 2015 increased the Horn’s strategic importance because Gulf states needed new military bases and personnel to sustain their campaign against the rebel group. The emirates opened a military base on the Eritrean coastline while Omar al-Bashir’s regime in Sudan sent tens of thousands of troops from the country’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces into Yemen to support the Saudi and Emirati efforts there.
At the same time, Middle Eastern countries had begun to doubt U.S. security commitments to the region amid the Obama administration’s widely publicized “pivot to Asia” and diplomacy with Iran, which accelerated their scramble to secure their own interests in a wider area. Middle Eastern governments became more anxious and competition among them grew more intense. A 2017 intra-Gulf crisis culminating in the blockade of Qatar by neighboring countries spilled directly into Africa, as loose blocs of patrons competed for influence and Saudi Arabia and the UAE pushed Horn leaders to choose a side. The UAE began to make increasingly ambitious political interventions in the Horn: for instance, it placed a major bet on the Ethiopian leader Abiy Ahmed, who rose to power in 2018, by backing his regime with an early infusion of $3 billion and providing critical military support when he faced a rebellion in the Tigray region.
The catastrophic war in Sudan further fused the Horn of Africa to the Middle East. When mass protests in 2019 threatened to topple Bashir’s regime in Khartoum, Abu Dhabi and Riyadh backed a military junta that seized power. After the junta’s two leaders turned on each other in 2023, the UAE emerged as the major patron of Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces, although Abu Dhabi formally denies the extent of its interventions. Saudi Arabia also had historic ties to the RSF and at first tried to mediate between the two sides, but the scope of the UAE’s intervention eventually led Riyadh to more firmly back the SAF. Saud Arabia has become the Sudanese army’s most important ally.
Over the past year, those disputes in the Horn of Africa began to spill back across the Red Sea. Tensions between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh over the war in Sudan appeared to contribute to the breakup of the Emirati-Saudi partnership to counter the Houthis. In December 2025, Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government demanded that the UAE pull out of the country after a sudden offensive near the Saudi border by separatist forces backed by the emirates. The same month, Israel became the first country to recognize the independence of Somaliland. Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and others in Africa and the Middle East fiercely opposed this move, but the UAE remained silent, deepening the tensions within the Gulf.
The Emirati-Saudi rift, exacerbated by Horn politics, hindered a collective Gulf response after the United States and Israel declared war on Iran in February. The war itself entangled the Horn and the Middle East only more tightly. Saudi Arabia sought to safeguard itself through new regional security pacts and diplomatic alignments, while the UAE strengthened its security partnerships with the United States and Israel. Although both sides try to downplay the extent of this rift in public, its effects are evident on the other side of the Red Sea, too.
Saudi Arabia has deepened its involvement in both Sudanese and Somali affairs, in coordination with Egypt and Turkey: such support appears to have driven the SAF’s recent gains on the battlefield and emboldened SAF leaders to continue to reject U.S. truce proposals. Meanwhile, the Somali government is expanding its partnerships with key Saudi allies, including Pakistan. Saudi Arabia and Egypt also oppose Ethiopia’s quest to regain a sovereign coastal port and naval presence on the Red Sea, and are bolstering their ties to Ethiopia’s coastal neighbors. (Saudi Arabia’s wish to control maritime security in the Red Sea has only grown since the U.S.-Israeli attack led Iran to throttle the Strait of Hormuz, forcing Riyadh to divert the bulk of its oil exports through the Bab el Mandeb Strait.)
Middle Eastern countries’ expanding involvement in the Horn increases the risk that internal conflicts in Ethiopia and Sudan will merge into a larger regional war zone. An infusion of Emirati military support for the RSF through Ethiopia has helped stoke distrust between Khartoum and Addis Ababa. Ethiopia, meanwhile, accuses the SAF of giving safe harbor to thousands of fighters loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, which in April effectively annulled a 2022 peace deal and retook power over Ethiopia’s Tigray region. In late September, with quiet backing from Eritrea, the TPLF launched large-scale offensives against the Ethiopian army, pushing the region back into war. By early October, the Ethiopian army had retaken Tigray’s regional capital, a move that may only force the fighting north toward the Eritrean-Ethiopian border. A new Eritrean-Ethiopian war would, in effect, pit Egypt and Saudi Arabia against the UAE.
In Somalia, meanwhile, long-standing political struggles are becoming increasingly entangled with the Middle East’s widening security conflicts. Israel’s recognition of Somaliland, which sits near the Bab el Mandeb Strait in the Gulf of Aden, caused deep alarm in Egypt, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia. In response, in early 2026, Mogadishu signed a formal defense cooperation agreement with Riyadh and canceled their existing security and economic deals with Abu Dhabi.
The UAE had already aligned with Somaliland by establishing key military infrastructure there and revamping a major port in Berbera; it also created a military outpost and took over a port, Bosaso, in the nearby semiautonomous Puntland region, which has been at odds with Somalia’s federal government for years. As the Houthis in Yemen have expanded their operations around the Bab el Mandeb Strait and refreshed their attacks on Saudi Arabia, they have also reportedly sought to develop their own inroads into the Horn, especially with the Islamist insurgent group al-Shabab, which controls swaths of southern Somalia. The Yemeni group has threatened to attack Somaliland should Israel establish a presence there, and U.S. officials have asserted that it is already sending al-Shabab weapons.
To some extent, the Middle East’s expansion into the Horn of Africa is filling a vacuum left by others. The United States’ general retrenchment from African diplomacy and aid has encouraged Horn leaders to look elsewhere for partnerships. They need to make up for specific exits: for more than 15 years, for instance, the United Nations provided logistical support for an African Union military deployment in Somalia to counter al-Shabab. The mission succeeding in helping take and hold territory. But in July, the Trump administration vowed to block the UN from giving logistical support to the mission. This move is likely to prompt even greater involvement by Turkey, the Somali government’s top backer, and other allied countries.
The Horn’s renewed integration with the greater Middle East is not inherently a negative trend. Horn leaders are right to want diverse allies. Investments by the Gulf’s state-directed economies have given Horn countries an economic lifeline, particularly when it comes to infrastructure. Middle East capitals can also serve as crucial hubs for mediating conflicts: in 2024, for instance, Erdogan mediated a détente between Ethiopia and Somalia.
But for now, those upsides are outweighed by the fact that integration of the two regions is occurring substantially through proxy warfare and arms. It was always unlikely that the Horn of Africa and the Middle East would remain as separate as they were during the twentieth century. Throughout much of history, the Red Sea connected societies on both shores, and today, geography is reasserting itself. The biggest danger arises if some Middle East governments continue to act as if they can back various warring factions in the Horn without absorbing the consequences, and if Horn governments seek Middle Eastern patronage mainly to arm themselves against local rivals.
Arresting this trajectory will require Saudi Arabia and the UAE to agree to work together to de-escalate conflict in the Horn before a new regional war erupts. As for Sudan, the two should step back from maximalist demands and press the respective belligerents to agree to a cease-fire and a transitional government. Saudi Arabia and the UAE also need to coordinate to prevent a new cross-border war involving Ethiopia: Abu Dhabi needs to discourage any push by Ethiopia to expand its war with the TPLF into Eritrea and all the way to the Red Sea coastline, while Riyadh should discourage its key allies Egypt, Eritrea, and Sudan from meddling inside Ethiopia. The two could work together to restart quiet talks between the Somali government in Mogadishu and Somaliland’s administration in Hargeisa about their long-running dispute. Leaders in the Horn itself, meanwhile, have experience managing hostile interstate relations so they simmer rather than explode into outright regional conflict. They should immediately call a regional summit among Horn heads of state and should also encourage a more collective approach toward regional security from their Middle East allies.
An alternative, darker version of integration is also visible. The Emiratis and Saudis could entrench their respective positions in the Horn even if the two capitals patch up some of their differences. Other rivalries among various Middle East powers—for instance, between Turkey and Qatar on the one side and Israel and the UAE on the other—could also exacerbate the Horn’s internal fault lines. One way or the other, the Horn of Africa’s return to the Middle East theater is likely irreversible. The question now is whether the various powers can find a way to manage their different interests to defuse conflict—or whether, conflict by conflict, they will continue to discover that wars launched on one side of the Red Sea no longer remain contained there, forcing millions of civilians throughout the Horn to pay the price.
articles.summary: Conflicts in the Middle East and the Horn of Africa have become inseparable.

articles.title: The Myth of Military Victory
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
Military victory is an alluring idea. A short, violent campaign that defeats the enemy promises payoffs at a tolerable price. The Trump administration expected such an outcome in Iran in February 2026. The Netanyahu government sought it in Gaza in October 2023, then in Lebanon and Iran. Russian President Vladimir Putin assumed his 2022 invasion of Ukraine would deliver it. Many critics of U.S. policy in Afghanistan and Iraq decry a failure to achieve military victory, contrasting such wars with the decisive battlefield outcomes they believe were achieved in the 1990–91 Gulf War and World War II. And until recently, the debate over U.S. aid to Ukraine featured widespread calls to help the country win a military victory, dismissing negotiations as appeasement.
Yet those who invoke the term rarely define it. “Victory” means achieving the political aims for which one went to war. But “military victory” implies more. The adjective signals that those aims are secured through combat rather than at the bargaining table. Negotiation requires compromise and invites stalling that can exhaust political will. Battlefield victory, by contrast, promises a prostrate enemy with no meaningful choice but to accept the victor’s terms on the victor’s timetable. That promise is what makes the idea so attractive and so ubiquitous.
But the notion of military victory is a dangerous myth. All modern wars end in negotiated settlements; talks are not a second-best fallback. To end a war, both sides must choose to stop fighting, and those choices always require nontrivial bargaining. Destruction matters, of course. It is what distinguishes war from peacetime politics. But its role is to shape the bargain, not to annihilate the enemy, which almost never happens.
The myth of military victory has repeatedly led governments to start or prolong wars on false premises about how those wars would end. The Trump administration believed force could compel Iran’s unconditional surrender; instead, the United States finds itself in a stalemate. The Netanyahu government’s conviction that it can defeat Hamas militarily has lengthened the Gaza war in pursuit of an unattainable goal. Putin’s expectation of battlefield victory in Ukraine has mired both countries in a war with no apparent endgame.
If Chinese leader Xi Jinping makes the same mistake, an attack on Taiwan could ensnare Beijing in a conflict that is easier to start than to stop, with stakes far beyond the Taiwan Strait. And if the United States assumes that it could secure a military victory in a war with China, then it, too, could find itself exhausted in a fight it cannot easily end.
Muddled thinking about how wars conclude also breeds prewar errors in intelligence, modernization, and force design. And misunderstanding the relationship between bargaining and fighting produces a systematic failure to integrate negotiating strategy with campaign planning. As long as policymakers do not grasp that wars end only when both sides are ready to lay down their arms, they will continue to be frustrated by the inability of military force to achieve their political goals.
No modern war has destroyed an enemy’s ability to resist. Combatants can always keep fighting if they choose, even after enemies sweep their military from the field or capture their capital. Such persistence can reverse fortunes and decide wars. Winning a war requires offering surviving (and potential) fighters a deal they prefer to continued resistance. These deals can be one-sided. But terms and bargaining always matter: no war ends unless both sides choose to accept a settlement and stop.
The only alternative is to physically annihilate one’s enemies. Rome succeeded in doing so when it ended the Third Punic War by enslaving Carthage’s surviving citizens and, according to legend, salting the city’s ruins so nothing would grow there again. But no war in the modern era has met this criterion, and few have come close. Since the Napoleonic Wars ended, in 1815, the defeated parties in interstate wars have lost a median of eight percent of their forces. In two-thirds of those cases, that figure was under ten percent. The only country to lose more than 90 percent of its forces was Paraguay, in the Triple Alliance War (1864–70). Most belligerents accept defeat—settlement on unfavorable terms—long before their capacity to resist runs out.
War-ending settlements can be explicit or tacit. Explicit negotiations involve direct communication, offers, and counteroffers; examples include the Korean War armistice and the 1995 Dayton accords that concluded the Bosnian war. Tacit bargaining uses actions, threats, or declarations to signal acceptance or rejection of terms without formal talks.
The 1990–91 Gulf War, for example, ended when the U.S.-led coalition announced a unilateral cease-fire, and the Iraqis stopped fighting, too, without diplomatic exchanges. Combat had shown Iraqi President Saddam Hussein that continued resistance would bring further coalition advances, potentially to Baghdad; the cease-fire signaled that U.S. and allied forces would hold their positions if the Iraqis did the same. Saddam understood and reciprocated. General Norman Schwarzkopf, the coalition commander, then instructed Baghdad to send a military delegation to Safwan airfield to negotiate disengagement. The result heavily favored the United States and its allies. They liberated Kuwait, their central aim. Saddam preserved his regime but lost his conquests and faced postwar restrictions, leaving him worse off than he was before his invasion.
This was an unambiguous victory, but it was not achieved by destroying Iraq’s capacity to resist. At the cease-fire, the Iraqi army retained most of its prewar strength. Up to 50,000 Iraqi soldiers had been killed and 75,000 wounded out of a force exceeding a million—under 15 percent. Over 800,000 troops survived and could have kept fighting. Days later, Iraqi forces crushed Shiite uprisings in the south.
Saddam’s decision to stop in 1991 was not a mere acceptance of reality. Iraq’s experience in its next war with the United States shows why. In 2003, the Iraqi military disintegrated after just seven weeks of fighting, its soldiers abandoning posts, weapons, and commanders and shedding their uniforms. By mid-May, Saddam could bring far less military power to bear than at Safwan in 1991. If a country could ever end a war by disarming the enemy, the United States should have done so in Iraq by May 2003. It did not.
The Iraqi military could no longer hold ground or resist coalition advances, but many of its soldiers carried on, even after Baghdad fell and their only option was to resort to irregular tactics. Sunni Baathists understood the implicit terms on offer: life under a U.S.-installed Shiite government. They preferred to fight on. The U.S. military suffered fewer than 3,000 casualties in 2003 but more than 33,000 in the next eight years. The insurgents failed to restore Saddam’s regime, but the war did not end in 2003, when Baghdad fell and its uniformed military evaporated.
Afghanistan offers a similar example. By mid-2002, the U.S. invasion had disarmed the Taliban’s military, occupied Kabul, and driven the group’s leaders from the country. Like Iraqi Baathists a year later, the Taliban faced a dominant enemy controlling their homeland, with no immediate prospect of retaking the capital. If “military victory” can terminate a war, then Afghanistan, too, should have been a decisive U.S. success. It was not. Taliban survivors rejected the terms on offer—an Afghan government that excluded them—even though their situation was far bleaker than Saddam’s in 1991. They kept fighting as irregulars, and by 2021 they had recaptured Kabul, driven out U.S. forces, and restored their rule.
The elusiveness of military victory does not make battlefield effectiveness irrelevant. But the purpose of fighting is to shape the two sides’ bargaining leverage by shifting their expectations of future costs, not to annihilate the enemy. Success in combat enables productive talks, but it is no substitute for them.
Perhaps the most frequently cited example of military victory—the imposition of a brute-force triumph on a prostrate enemy—is the Allied conquest of Nazi Germany and imperial Japan in World War II. In conflicts from Afghanistan to Ukraine to Gaza, policymakers and pundits invoke Germany’s and Japan’s ostensible military destruction in direct contrast to wars that ended with negotiated outcomes. Yet World War II did not end because the vanquished had no choice but surrender. The fighting did not disarm Germany or Japan. Both retained the capacity to inflict enormous casualties on the Allies, and neither surrendered unconditionally. The victors offered explicit terms—conditions—to both. These concessions were small, and the Allies unambiguously won. But even World War II ended in bargains between actors with options.
Imperial Japan fielded nearly eight million troops during the war. Fewer than two million died in combat. When Japan surrendered, in August 1945, more than six million armed, equipped, uniformed, and commanded soldiers remained in the field. These forces could not reclaim Japan’s conquests, which the Allies had steadily reversed since mid-1942. By the summer of 1945, the United States had driven the Japanese navy into port and severed Tokyo’s control of airspace and sea-lanes, leaving the Allies poised to invade Japan and depose Emperor Hirohito.
Yet Japan continued to resist—not because it expected to destroy the Allied militaries, or reconquer lost territory, or throw an invasion force into the sea, but because it sought to secure more tolerable settlement terms by threatening to kill more servicemen than the Allies were willing to sacrifice. Japan retained significant leverage. At Okinawa, which fell in June 1945, Japanese forces inflicted 50,000 casualties on U.S. troops. In August, the U.S. War Department estimated that invading Japan would cost hundreds of thousands more. Japanese leaders understood this and hoped the prospect would persuade the Americans to soften their terms. It did.
The Allies had demanded “unconditional surrender” at the Casablanca conference in January 1943 but never defined what that meant. Officials in Tokyo assumed it included dismantling the imperial system and imprisoning the emperor. For over two years, Japan fought on rather than accept such an outcome.
On July 26, 1945, ahead of the planned November invasion of Japan, the Allies issued the Potsdam Declaration. Although it again called for “unconditional” surrender, the document offered multiple explicit conditions. Japan would retain sovereignty over its four main islands. Its military personnel would return home without internment. The country would keep its industry, and its people would not be subject to forced labor. It would also gain access to raw materials and trade. The declaration did not, in fact, demand unconditional surrender; instead, it articulated conditions for surrender.
Most important, the declaration was silent on the emperor’s status, reflecting extensive debate among U.S. government officials. Some, such as Secretary of State James Byrnes, advocated an explicit demand that Hirohito be prosecuted for war crimes. Others, such as Secretary of War Henry Stimson, argued that this would prolong the war and favored letting Hirohito remain on the throne. The final document compromised by saying nothing on the subject. Stimson hoped Japan would understand this omission as an implicit offer to preserve the monarchy, and he was right. Tokyo interpreted this silence as a signal that the emperor could remain. Hirohito served as emperor until his death, in 1989.
This concession was modest but not trivial. Regime change remained the Allies’ central goal, but it was never the only one. The entire U.S. war cabinet valued prosecuting the emperor. Some members would sacrifice this aim to end the conflict; others would not. Sparing Hirohito meant giving up an objective that mattered less than regime change, but one that still mattered.
Holding out for this concession cost Japan dearly. Accepting the pre-Potsdam terms a few months earlier would have saved hundreds of thousands of lives and averted the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Yet Tokyo did manage to coerce a change in the Allies’ offer, and as a result, its surrender was not unconditional. The defeat of Japan was a one-sided bargain, not a military victory imposed on an opponent without agency.
Germany presents a similar case. When it surrendered, in May 1945, the Wehrmacht still fielded more than three million armed and actively resisting soldiers. German forces had been losing ground since the Battle of Stalingrad, in 1943, and by early 1945, the Allies were advancing deep into the Reich. Yet the German army kept fighting, inflicting severe casualties until the very end. In the Battle of Berlin, waged in April and May, more than 360,000 Soviet troops were killed, wounded, or reported missing.
The Wehrmacht’s millions of surviving troops could have melted into the countryside, turned to insurgency, and fought on after Berlin fell—as the Afghan Taliban and Iraqi Baathists would do decades later. Hitler’s inner circle had considered doing just that and developed written plans for guerrilla resistance. Yet his successors chose to stop the war and signed the instrument of surrender on May 7. As with Japan, this was a choice, and the Germans could have chosen differently. Instead, their leaders decided that the terms on offer were preferable to the cost of a protracted struggle that Germany was fully capable of conducting.
Although highly one-sided, the terms Germany accepted did not amount to unconditional surrender. The Allies offered explicit conditions, which they softened in early 1945 to persuade the Germans to lay down their arms. That autumn, U.S. policymakers had proposed the Morgenthau Plan for postwar Germany. Originally outlined by Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau, it sought to render the country incapable of future aggression by deindustrializing it, disarming it, and dividing it into impoverished rump states. The plan would strip the country of its factories, internationalize the industrial Ruhr Valley, resettle the region’s workforce elsewhere, destroy its mines, force German civilians into labor abroad, and expropriate German assets.
When the plan leaked in September 1944, the Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels seized on it to rally the German public. If this was what the Allies would do, he argued, then Germans had to resist to the last cartridge. He instructed German forces in the city of Aachen, then under American attack, to make “every house . . . a fortress.” Blaming the city’s fanatical resistance on the Morgenthau Plan, Allied officials publicly repudiated it and softened their position. At Yalta in February 1945, U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt declared, “It is not our purpose to destroy the people of Germany.” The eventual surrender terms omitted deindustrialization, forced labor, and permanent economic destruction. In the war’s final weeks, the Allies added explicit conditions: Germany would avoid annexation, remain independent (although not sovereign or unitary), and rely on armed German citizens for policing.
These conditions were modest. The Allies clearly won. Germany forfeited all its war aims, suffered occupation, and remained partitioned for 45 years. Yet the terms on which the war ended were not trivial. The Allies wanted the Nazi regime gone, but that was not all they wanted. The status of post-Nazi Germany mattered greatly to Germans and Americans alike.
Roosevelt preferred a punitive peace that would humble and permanently weaken Germany; he settled for a more generous outcome because his first-choice model was apparently unacceptable to the Germans. Intense deliberation produced this decision, reflecting a conscious effort to ease conditions that Allied leaders judged to be too harsh. Germany accepted terms that offered at least some postwar guarantees, once the signatories understood that the Allies no longer intended to cripple Germany forever. The result was a one-sided and tacit coercive bargain, but a bargain all the same.
