articles.title: The Triumph of Tech-Fueled Propaganda
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
RENÉE DIRESTA is an Associate Research Professor at the McCourt School of Public Policy at Georgetown University. She is the author of Invisible Rulers: The People Who Turn Lies Into Reality.
JOSH A. GOLDSTEIN is a Nonresident Research Fellow at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.
In April and May, hundreds of users of the social media platform Bluesky discovered that their accounts had been hijacked and used to spread content about Ukraine. Researchers at Clemson University later attributed the campaign to the Social Design Agency, a Russian consulting firm sanctioned by the U.S. Department of Treasury for running Kremlin-directed malign influence campaigns. The Bluesky effort turned out to be only one piece of the SDA’s much larger portfolio of recent operations: leaked documents obtained by the news portal Delfi Estonia and shared with the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project revealed plans for real-world acts of vandalism, intimidation, and election interference.
Most discussions of online influence and disinformation campaigns assume that attacks such as the one on Bluesky are discrete efforts. But as the SDA’s operations show, influence operations are increasingly interconnected and part of propaganda strategies that transcend traditional boundaries. Sophisticated states such as China, Iran, and Russia routinely combine overt public messaging with covert influence and mix broadcast channels with social media platforms. State media outlets, official government accounts, paid influencers, fake personas, hacked accounts, and bot armies are parts of the same system. This integrated approach, which we call “full-spectrum propaganda,” is now the norm for U.S. adversaries trying to spread their message abroad.
In full-spectrum propaganda, as we outlined in a recent Security Studies article, the many channels that states can use reinforce each other, making narratives seem more credible and allowing them to proliferate more widely. A story publicized on a state-backed broadcast channel may reach one audience, while social media accounts catch the attention of another. Official outlets can quote from posts on fake accounts whose creators masquerade as ordinary members of the public, making a fringe claim seem normal. Paid influencers can tailor messages in a style that resonates with niche audiences. The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence is making this strategy even more powerful: states are increasingly integrating AI into every level of their propaganda operations, allowing small groups or individuals to conduct propaganda campaigns that would previously have required far greater resources.
Strategies that merely address discrete foreign influence campaigns will fail to meet the challenges presented by full-spectrum propaganda. The United States needs to be able to understand, assess, and counter influence operations holistically, yet as the threat grows, the United States has been undercutting the capacity that would allow it to do so. Politicians have been dismantling the government agencies designed to track foreign influence, and social media companies are raising barriers to research on their platforms, leaving the country unprepared. As AI accelerates the spread and expands the reach of global propaganda, Washington is blinding itself to the challenge.
For much of the last decade, politicians and the public understood foreign influence operations on social media through the parts that first became visible. Most often, this would be a network of fake accounts discovered by social media companies as part of their efforts to eliminate bots, scams, and online deception on their platforms. After taking down such accounts, companies would write reports and researchers (including us) would publish analyses to explain the evolving tactics, techniques, and procedures of online influence campaigns. The focus on the specifics of each individual operation led people to think of the threats as narrow, distinct incidents.
But the fragment of what is visible is not the whole story. State-backed propagandists do not have to choose between state media and fake accounts, between covert personas and overt broadcasters, or between a spoofed media outlet or a Telegram channel. They can use all of them together—and they are increasingly doing so.
The SDA, for instance, documented its own work in the style of a consultancy reporting to a client. That client, the leaked documents suggest, was the administration of Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose officials appear in the agency’s internal communications overseeing its work. The consulting firm’s covert operations are just one component of a much broader Russian propaganda apparatus that also includes state media networks, official government channels, and fake personas. Moscow and its proxies use all of these tools in tandem to amplify propaganda messages and reach many types of audiences.
As the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project and other news outlets explained, the SDA was behind a fake video in June 2025, branded to appear as if it were made by the Saudi media outlet Al Arabiya, which claimed that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky purchased a luxury apartment in Burj Khalifa, a skyscraper in Dubai. An internal report estimated that this false story could have logged as many as 86 million views globally; a similar SDA effort targeting Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan likely racked up over ten million views. In some cases, rather than mimicking an existing outlet such as Al Arabiya, SDA conjures fully branded fake news outlets: one leaked document described plans to use an outlet tied to the SDA in Armenia’s June parliamentary elections.
When more distance is required, SDA turns to paid influencers. Earlier this year, for example, the Kremlin wanted to support the reelection bid of Viktor Orban, then Hungary’s prime minister. According to the Financial Times, the SDA, recognizing that overt support from Russia could be interpreted as foreign meddling and hurt Orban’s campaign, proposed contacting local influencers via go-betweens to make the Russian content appear homegrown.
The SDA even bridges the gap between the real world and online information by staging controversial or threatening events to generate attention. In September 2025, severed pig heads, including several marked “Macron” for the French president, were left outside mosques and Islamic centers in and around Paris. The leaked SDA files reveal the meticulous plans behind the effort, along with similar vandalism plots elsewhere in France and in Germany. Mainstream broadcast and social media covered these events, generating real-world concern about xenophobia and Islamophobia in Europe. The SDA calls these “cognitive strikes”: the point is securing visibility, shaping perceptions, and creating emotional responses that can be exploited.
Such covert activity complements Moscow’s efforts to continue to develop its broadcast propaganda apparatus worldwide. In 2025, the Kremlin allocated 31 billion rubles ($367 million) to RT, the Russian state broadcaster. RT and Sputnik, the state news agency and radio service, have expanded across Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia, according to the BBC, including by taking over local media channels. RT Academy, the broadcaster’s educational arm, ran a journalism program in Jakarta, the Indonesian capital, to train a new generation of reporters; its programming included “fact checking” and “applying ethical standards” in storytelling. RT is not only broadcasting on its own stations but is also funding and operating sympathetic proxy channels. In 2024, for example, the U.S. Department of Justice indicted two RT employees for funneling nearly $10 million to Tenet Media, a right-wing U.S. media outlet. Even influencers working for Tenet Media were unaware of the source of that funding.
Full-spectrum propaganda presents a distinct challenge because it exploits the way modern information systems confer legitimacy. As research in psychology has shown, repetition reinforces belief, and a narrative may seem more believable when it appears in multiple distinct places or when many seemingly unconnected people start talking about it. A claim looks more credible when an outlet, a few influencers, and some individuals in a Telegram channel seem to arrive at the same conclusion independently.
Integrated propaganda campaigns can also more easily evade existing crackdown efforts by individual platforms. Because social media companies differ in how they regulate content, when fake accounts on one site get removed, they may simply respawn or migrate to platforms with more permissible policies or weaker enforcement capacity. When Russian officials and state media outlets portrayed the bombing of a Ukrainian maternity hospital in March 2022 as a faked event and claimed that the victims were paid actors, social media platforms such as Twitter took down the deceptive content. But anonymous Telegram channels claiming to be fact-checking organizations gained popularity and spread the false narrative there. Some of these efforts may have been genuine attempts to investigate the charges, but many others appeared to be the work of state-backed propaganda groups seeking new places to share their message.
In a world of full-spectrum propaganda, then, looking at foreign influence campaigns on a platform-by-platform basis or simply as a social media problem is too limited. Merely analyzing posts on Bluesky, for instance, overlooks the way the message they are promoting connects to simultaneous efforts on Facebook and X, articles in state media, and public broadcasts around the world. Understanding a modern propaganda campaign requires examining where else a narrative may have appeared, whether fake outlets were quoted by influencers, whether ostensibly independent sources were connected, and how those different parts of the system reinforce one another.
AI is further transforming propaganda strategies and making the challenge of countering it harder. An investigation by The New York Times revealed that China and Iran have used Chinese open-source models to run propaganda campaigns through AI agents with limited human supervision. The agents created fake accounts on a variety of social media networks, posted false stories, and coordinated their messaging. Although these examples were limited in reach, they are likely harbingers of what is to come. State media channels are also using AI to expand their reach: Anthropic found that the Russian state media had used its AI model, Claude, to turn Romanian and Moldovan news into Russian-language articles, showing how states can easily translate content without needing linguistic expertise. Propagandists are even targeting the AI systems themselves to try to shape the answers that chatbots provide. They are creating fake websites and publishing content designed to come to the surface when AI models retrieve information and to influence the data that trains AI models on how to respond.
Because U.S. adversaries are pursuing a full-spectrum, AI-optimized approach to propaganda, Washington needs as much capacity as it can get to assess the threat holistically and expose or combat it. Unfortunately, social media platforms and the U.S. government have spent the past several years dismantling exactly that capacity, leaving the United States unaware of its vulnerabilities.
In Silicon Valley, companies have made it harder to access data about their platforms, limiting the visibility of propaganda campaigns. Social media platforms have walked back platform integrity and transparency commitments and dissolved collaborations with researchers. In May, Meta laid off ten percent of its workforce, including members of its investigations team, which had been instrumental in combating online influence operations. In 2024, Meta eliminated CrowdTangle, a transparency tool that researchers could use to gain access to public posts, and in 2023, Twitter, now known as X, ended free access to its API for researchers, who had used it to study public posts on the platform. X now charges them $5 for access to every 1,000 tweets, or at least $42,000 per month for an enterprise subscription, making it far too costly for many academics to conduct research on the platform at scale.
These barriers have limited independent checks on statements from the platforms and the government about foreign influence, making it harder to identify the severity of such campaigns and draw useful lessons from them. When in August, X announced the removal of 200,000 accounts from a suspected Chinese bot farm—200 of which it claimed posted information about AI data centers—the company did not make data about the operation available to researchers. Politicians seized on the news to blame Chinese covert influence for the backlash to data centers in the United States, but an analysis conducted by Clemson University professor Darren Linvill revealed that posts from the accounts that could be identified had received virtually no engagement and were not a source of significant influence.
In Washington, a focus on fighting domestic censorship has led to the dissolution of institutions leading U.S. efforts to track foreign influence campaigns. U.S. President Donald Trump’s executive order on ending censorship, signed on his first day in office in January 2025, was framed as an attempt to prevent the government from infringing on constitutionally protected speech. But the result has been to stifle federal efforts to mitigate foreign influence, and claims of censorship have been used to shut down or weaken essential institutions. In 2024, Congress failed to extend the mandate for the State Department’s Global Engagement Center, an office set up in 2016 with bipartisan support and a goal of tracking propaganda from China, Iran, Russia, and other foreign actors. The organization created to replace it, the Counter Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference hub, was then shut down by the State Department. Republican lawmakers and other critics who campaigned against these offices claimed that they were trying to censor Americans, but no courts ultimately found that they had.
Then, in August 2025, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard closed the Foreign Malign Influence Center, which coordinated the intelligence community’s analysis of foreign interference and methods for countering it. The Justice Department also shut down the FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force, which sought to expose illegal foreign interference on U.S. soil and aligned investigations and intelligence sharing within and across agencies. Taken together, the destruction of these institutions has created a huge gap in the knowledge available to people in Washington about what China, Iran, and Russia are doing, especially the entire spectrum of influence activities they are undertaking. As Senator Mark Warner, vice chairman of the Select Committee on Intelligence, warned this spring, too little capacity remains to track or disrupt covert campaigns run by adversaries of the United States. At the same time that foreign influence operations are becoming more integrated, the U.S. government is losing the coordination needed to understand them.
As the United States blinds itself, foreign adversaries are expanding their efforts. Influence operations will increasingly involve AI-enhanced systems and organizations that can autonomously create fake news outlets, generate articles and videos, disseminate them through hijacked or inauthentic accounts, seed them among influencers, quote them in official state media, and trick AI answer engines into thinking that fallacies or outright lies represent the truth or mainstream opinion. As China, Iran, and Russia operate across the full spectrum of propaganda, the United States is getting stuck in narrow silos. Without the capacity to even understand the nature of the threat, Washington cannot begin to counter it.
articles.summary: America isn’t ready for the next wave of foreign influence operations.

articles.title: China’s Long Twilight
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
During the boom years of the reform era, from 1978 to the early 2000s, China was a country of productive workers. The working-age population (those aged 15 to 64) rose from 57 percent of the population in 1978 to a peak of nearly 75 percent in 2010. They built the roads, factories, apartment complexes, and firms that powered three decades of close to ten percent annual growth—a 20-fold economic expansion.
But over the past decade, this tide has turned. Beijing’s one-child policy, plus the same social forces that have dragged East Asian fertility to historic lows, have produced below-replacement birth rates for three decades in China—draining the fuel that powered China’s rise. China’s total population peaked at 1.4 billion in 2021 and is now falling by three to four million people per year—roughly equivalent to losing one Los Angeles each year. By the 2040s, if China continues to follow East Asia’s descent to ultralow fertility rates, it will shed around one percent of its population annually—roughly ten million people, more than the population of New York City. At the same time, the proportion of China’s population aged 65 and older will surge, doubling from 15 percent today to around 30 percent in the 2040s, and then rising to well over 40 percent by the late twenty-first century. The size of that cohort in the United States, by contrast, is projected to rise far more gradually, from around 19 percent of the population today to just over 23 percent in 2060.
Put simply, China is entering a century of demographic decline. This change will remake the country’s economy and politics just as dramatically as the last century’s demographic boom did. Back in the mid-twentieth century, improvements in health and falling infant mortality rates led to a burgeoning youth population, which Mao Zedong channeled into revolutionary social change, overturning entrenched hierarchies and remaking society from the bottom up. By 1978, China had a swelling population of working-age adults, and Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping’s pragmatic policies of “reform and opening up” astutely plugged them into the global economy, allowing China to emerge as the world’s factory.
Today, as the population rapidly grays, China’s political system is becoming increasingly regressive and rigid. As the Chinese Communist Party pivots back toward one-man rule, its vaunted institutions of technocratic rule are not what they once were. Instead of creatively addressing emerging challenges, the CCP is relying on repression and reflexively following central mandates—no matter the risks. Economically, for instance, policymakers continue to pursue Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s preferred export-driven industrial policy despite the obvious need to boost domestic consumption and strengthen the social security net for the poor.
The story of twenty-first-century China, then, is not just one of demographic decline but also one of political paralysis—and what happens when those two intersect. It is this combination that makes China’s future especially bleak. As China ages, the social pressures bearing down on its political system will only intensify. Mid-twenty-first-century China could end up looking a lot like the sixteenth-century Ming dynasty, a sclerotic political regime rendered increasingly brittle by worsening social, gender, and generational divides. Lest observers in Washington gloat about this fate, however, China’s trajectory is ultimately a warning: demographic decline and political erosion can hollow out any great power—including the United States.
As the journalist Li Yuan has observed, the United States suffers from China envy. Tech investors fawn over its latest AI models. Energy specialists are awestruck by its industrial dominance in batteries and solar power. And journalists and analysts often return from visits offering rosy-eyed panegyrics about China’s gleaming transit systems and engineering capacity. Politicians and pundits, meanwhile, often fuse China’s expanding navy and missile tests with Xi’s speeches on “the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation” to form a single image: a strong state successfully executing a grand strategy for its twenty-first-century rise.
Compared with the political circus in Washington and the malaise in the rest of America, such surface-level manifestations of China’s wealth and power often lead to sweeping conclusions about relative national trajectories. But on closer inspection, Beijing is also undergoing profound political erosion—it just doesn’t look like the process playing out in Washington. Because China’s system is tightly controlled, its descent into personalistic one-man rule does not play out in divisive confrontations on television or erratic social media rants by the top leader. Beijing’s transformation is instead happening quietly but just as consequentially. Over the past two decades, the CCP has come to revolve ever more tightly around a single man. Xi successfully lifted the constitutional term limits on his rule as state president in 2018 and swept clean the top ranks of the party itself at the 20th Party Congress, in 2022, packing them with his own supporters and yes men. Similar purges have regularly rocked the top ranks of China’s military, culminating in 2026, with the removal of Zhang Youxia, Xi’s own handpicked top general, leaving Xi virtually alone at the helm of China’s armed services.
Xi is now set to assume a fourth five-year term as party general secretary in 2027 and has given no sign as to who might take his place in 2032, when he will be 79 years old. An aged, isolated leader increases the risks of policy missteps in China, just as it does in the United States. But China’s slide from an efficient technocratic state into lifetime rule under an aging autocrat underscores a fundamental reality about the two countries’ trajectories: unlike China, the United States can still choose differently—in the midterm elections, in 2028, and every few years thereafter. China’s politics, by contrast, are far more stagnant.
Most critically, the stifling political atmosphere Xi has created is draining Beijing’s ability to respond to emerging problems as earlier generations once did. Back in the 1970s and 1980s, Chinese leaders under Deng were able to kickstart China’s era of rapid growth through rural reforms that completely reworked Maoist economic orthodoxy. As Zhao Shukai, a key party official involved in those reforms, has noted, Beijing’s ability to do so depended on a degree of “openness in the political structure, both in top-level power relations and in the ideological sphere.” That same era of flexibility saw party leaders empower competent and efficient officials to boldly address other pressing economic challenges, such as when General Secretary Jiang Zemin charged Premier Zhu Rongji with overhauling the tax system in 1994 to put China’s central finances on a firmer footing.
As Chinese politics regress, such flexible problem solving is giving way to rigid orthodoxy. Cadres now find themselves pressed to dogmatically pursue Xi’s signature policies regardless of the consequences. Back in 2022, for instance, Shanghai officials under Li Qiang, then municipal party secretary, abandoned their tentative efforts at a lighter, targeted approach to handling the spreading Omicron variant of COVID-19 when it became clear that such a policy would conflict with the “zero COVID” policies on which Xi had staked his personal legitimacy. The result was a brutal, two-month lockdown of Shanghai that left many without reliable access to food and medicine, and which became the template for lockdowns throughout China later that year. Rather than being censured for the debacle, however, Li was elevated by Xi to the top ranks of the Politburo Standing Committee in 2022 and made state premier in 2023. He now loyally leads Chinese officials on Xi’s push for industrial manufacturing and an export-driven growth strategy, despite concerns from economists about deflation, mounting overcapacity, and declining consumption.
Xi is not solely responsible for the stultifying inertia that is spreading in China’s society and state. Ever since the “color revolutions” of the early 2000s in post-Soviet states and the Arab Spring in 2010, party elites have grown more fearful of social unrest. Chinese authorities have tightened their grip on the media, the legal profession, and civil society, limiting the space for Chinese citizens to discuss mounting social woes and extinguishing emerging calls for deeper political reform. Space within the ranks of the CCP itself has similarly constricted, with few now willing to consider reforms that might seriously affect the vested interests of entrenched social groups. Back in the 1990s, by contrast, Zhu pushed through the wrenching restructuring of state-owned enterprises to secure China’s 2001 entry into the World Trade Organization—even though it threw tens of millions out of work and fueled massive labor protests. Accepting such short-term pain in pursuit of long-term gain was once considered one of China’s defining advantages, but Beijing today shows little comparable appetite for such measures.
Consider the party’s hesitancy in addressing the financial ramifications of China’s demographic decline. For decades, China’s retirement ages were among the lowest in the world: 60 years old for men, 55 for white-collar women, and 50 for blue-collar women. Unsurprisingly, Chinese researchers have predicted that the main urban pension fund covering some 500 million urban workers, retirees, and cadres will be exhausted by the mid-2030s. Raising the retirement age has thus been on Beijing’s to-do list for well over a decade. Yet authorities have moved extraordinarily slowly and timidly. Even though a phased increase was finally announced in 2024, it will not be fully implemented until 2040 and will still leave China with among the lowest retirement ages in the world: 63 for men, 58 for white-collar women, and 55 for blue-collar women.
Similarly, the CCP has put off addressing the stark inequality in benefits between urban and rural residents. Xi’s much-touted “common prosperity” campaign did little to narrow the gap between China’s rich and poor, nor did it address the wide discrepancies in state pension and health-care systems. In 2022, some 138 million urban retirees drew an average pension of $6,080 per year, roughly 18 times more than the meager $345 received by China’s 175 million rural and migrant retirees. Chinese scholars and officials regularly call for improving the benefits provided to rural residents as a means to stimulate domestic demand. But the reason genuinely redistributive measures have not been implemented is simple: party officials fear alienating the urban beneficiaries of the current system—civil servants, state employees, and middle-class urbanites, many with direct ties to the party itself—far more than the marginalized rural and migrant communities, which have limited capacity to mobilize.
These twin trends—an aging Leninist system sliding toward one-man rule and mounting political inertia in the face of anything that might trigger social unrest—have eroded China’s governance capacity. Even as the country heads toward a demographic cliff, Beijing seems incapable of preparing for the social challenges it will face in the decades ahead. China can build new high-speed rail lines or aircraft carriers but not, it seems, a sustainable social safety net for its rapidly graying countryside.
Political paralysis is only part of the story. Beijing is also actively steering China toward a reactionary version of itself that will worsen its demographic woes rather than help address them. With Xi’s dire warnings of foreign cultural infiltration, his demands that officials look to China’s “excellent traditional culture” in fusing Marxism with Confucian norms, and his praise for “women’s special role” as “virtuous wives and good mothers,” Beijing is stoking a nativist, neotraditionalist revival and reasserting patriarchal gender norms.
Beijing’s emerging worldview echoes that of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644). After a century of Mongol rule, the Ming dynasty began with a brief excursion into the outside world in the form of the famed treasure fleets of the early fifteenth century. But then the Ming pivoted toward an insular and reflexively conservative vision of China. Mongol rule had been deeply humiliating, and Ming leaders grew suspicious of foreign influence. They worked to restore what they saw as authentic Chinese civilization.
The parallels with today aren’t hard to find. In the Ming era, for instance, foreign beliefs such as Manichaeism, a Persian faith that had flourished under Mongol rule, were suppressed. Similarly, since 2010, Beijing has steadily departed from the more relaxed policies of the reform era and pursued the Sinicization of faiths such as Christianity and Islam. And ethnic minorities during the Ming dynasty were pressured into intermarriage, just as the 2026 Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress codifies Beijing’s new policies on forcible ethnic assimilation.
The Ming dynasty also saw a pivot back toward neo-Confucianism and its restrictive views of women’s roles in the family—views similar to the talking points currently being handed down by central authorities to the official All-China Women’s Federation: “Do a good job in family work and give full play to the unique role of women in promoting the family virtues of the Chinese nation and establishing good family customs, which is an important task assigned to the Women’s Federation by the Party Central Committee in the new era.”
This Ming dynasty redux will exacerbate China’s demographic problems. Plunging marriage and fertility rates across East Asia reflect deep tensions between women’s aspirations and society’s calcified gender norms. Between 2013 and 2024, new marriages in China fell by roughly 55 percent, as women and men alike backed away from family formation. Yet the all-male Politburo, one of China’s top party institutions, seems to think that addressing this trend is merely a question of finding the right incentives to push citizens toward marriage and children. In 2021, it launched a new slate of pro-natalist initiatives including baby bonuses and parental leave policies while restricting access to divorce, abortion, and vasectomies. It also reworked stamps, textbooks, and public art to showcase multichild families as ideal. Unsurprisingly, the tone-deaf and regressive nature of Beijing’s policies and language not only has had little impact but is also worsening China’s gender relations.
If Beijing can’t persuade its own citizens to have children, it might use a lever that other graying societies have used to address the challenges posed by rapid aging: immigration. Throughout the world, rapidly aging countries have resorted to foreign labor to fill jobs left vacant by shrinking workforces and to care for surging elderly populations. Even once insular South Korea is welcoming more migrant workers to make up for its low birthrate. Foreign residents now make up roughly five percent of its population, up from near zero in the early 1990s.
The CCP’s embrace of nativism, however, makes this option difficult. Census results in both 2010 and 2020 revealed that foreign residents made up 0.1 percent of China’s total population—roughly the same percentage as Taiwan or South Korea in 1990. But whereas those two societies turned toward greater openness in the following decades, China is heading down an increasingly ethnocentric path. Over the past decade, Chinese authorities have cracked down on foreign cultural products such as films, and since 2016 they have designated April 15 as National Security Day, which is marked by propaganda banners, school activities, and TV programs warning citizens to be on the watch for foreign spies. This messaging will not only make it harder to attract the foreign workers that China needs in the years ahead, such as eldercare workers. It is also priming the Chinese population to resist them.
In August 2025, authorities announced a new visa aimed at attracting young, talented foreigners working in STEM fields. This was consistent with Xi’s stated goals of making China a world leader in manufacturing and technology and competing with developed countries for global talent. But the popular backlash was immediate and furious. China’s youth unemployment rate stood at 18.9 percent that same month, and young people took to social media to rail against the government for selling out their interests. Posts on the topic racked up tens of millions of views in mere days. Some commentators who defended the government were called “race traitors.” Others speculated that Indian tech workers might surge into China and compete for jobs or marriage partners. More than a year later, there have been no reports of any such visa having been issued.
Domestic resentment toward “outsiders” presents yet another dangerous divide emerging in twenty-first-century China. China is not simply aging; it is likely to approach the centennial of its founding in 2049 with core social cleavages—between men and women, Chinese people and foreigners, urban and rural residents—deepened and embittered by decades of stagnant governance and backward-looking values. By midcentury, Beijing will be chronically short of the workers it needs, and it will likely end up on the wrong side of a new kind of populist discontent.
For some American policymakers, the top risk of these trends is war. In their 2022 book Danger Zone: The Coming Conflict With China, Hal Brands and Michael Beckley warn that demographic decline could push a “peaking China” to roll the dice and try to seize Taiwan before rising social pressures and economic constraints begin to bite in earnest. Such a fear is not absurd. A more apt framing, however, is not a rational, calculated gamble, but a severe miscalculation by an aging, isolated leader. As with Russian President Vladimir Putin before he decided to invade Ukraine in 2022, or with U.S. President Donald Trump before he launched a war with Iran in 2026, an elderly Xi could very well find himself insulated from reality, surrounded by cowed subordinates, and stumbling into catastrophe.
But the deeper risk for China is internal. In the near term, as current trend lines continue, China is poised for political stasis. It will likely make no serious efforts to address the woes of rural areas or to cut the benefits of privileged groups. A generation of youth will experience anemic economic growth and weaker job prospects compared with those of their parents, amid a stagnant political climate that is increasingly hostile to women in particular, all of which will result in people further opting out of marriage and family formation. As China ages, such trends will produce rising discontent, and China’s state apparatus will be steadily drawn into using comprehensive surveillance and “grid management” techniques—methods developed to contain ethnic minorities in Xinjiang and disgruntled petitioners throughout China—to handle it.
Indeed, Chinese authorities have already begun refashioning the tools of their security state in response. In 2023, Beijing created the Central Social Work Department and charged it with monitoring those suffering from any of the “four lacks” (no spouse or children, no job or stable income, no normal social interactions, or no financial assets, such as a house or car) or any of the “five losses” (failed investments, career or life setbacks, emotional imbalances, mental illness, or failed personal relationships). Beijing views such individuals as potential security threats capable of mass attacks, such as the November 2024 rampage in which a 62-year-old man, dissatisfied with the property settlement after his divorce, drove his car into a crowd and killed dozens.
The coming decades will see Beijing steadily “securitize” all the social problems arising from China’s demographic shifts. In the 2030s, aging party leaders living in rarefied Zhongnanhai compounds may look out and see superficial stability. Chinese tech billionaires may convince themselves that they, too, are immune from the concerns of the rabble. But increased repression and surveillance are not a long-term solution. These privileged few will be sitting on a time bomb of their own making, similar to that faced by political and economic elites during the waning years of the Ming dynasty.
By the late 1500s, the once vigorous Ming was severely eroding. Decades of fiscal profligacy, including the costs of an extended conflict with Japan in Korea, had drained the imperial treasury. Reformist officials such as Zhang Juzheng attempted to plug the hole in state finances, pushing through a series of reforms in an effort to broaden the tax base and force the gentry and landed elites to shoulder a larger share of the mounting fiscal burden. But the gentry fought back. After Zhang’s death, in 1582, they successfully unwound his reforms, posthumously disgracing him as a warning to others who might seek to target their privileges and wealth. The financial burden of an empire in distress fell instead on ordinary peasants.
Simultaneously, the Ming court slid into political paralysis. The Wanli emperor (1572–1620) spent two decades of his reign locked in an extended standoff with his own bureaucracy over the question of who would succeed him. The result: a political vacuum at the top. With the throne disengaged from governance, petitions and reports from officials piled up unread, crucial state posts went unfilled, and the imperial bureaucracy splintered amid poisonous factional infighting.
articles.summary: Demographic decline, political paralysis, and the fate of great powers.

articles.title: Brazil’s Election Won’t Fix What’s Broken
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
MATIAS SPEKTOR is Professor of Politics and International Relations at Fundação Getulio Vargas in São Paulo.
The Brazilian presidential election, which kicks off with a first round of voting on October 4, gives citizens a choice between radically different visions of politics. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, the standard-bearer of the Latin American left, seeks a fourth presidential term against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of Jair Bolsonaro, the hard-right former president who was sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting to overturn the results of the previous presidential election. The race is also a contest over how Brazil should conduct its foreign affairs: Lula emphasizes strategic autonomy, including through growing ties with China and other partners, while Flávio Bolsonaro favors close alignment with the Trump administration in the United States.
What unites the two candidates is the assumption that Brazil still has the freedom to choose its foreign policy strategy. Brazil’s vast resources, distance from active conflict, and influx of foreign direct investment should position it well to manage current global upheaval and great-power competition, and to effectively bargain for what it wants. But despite these valuable geopolitical assets, Brazil is losing global influence, and its autonomy to act is at risk. Major powers, including both China and the United States, are increasingly able to dictate their terms of engagement with Brazil. The country is also becoming isolated in South America, where it had until recently led the creation of regional institutions such as the trading bloc Mercosur. Its relationship with Argentina, for instance—which had helped underpin four decades of regional stability—has deteriorated to the point that neither country has an ambassador in the other’s capital.
Brazil is largely responsible for its waning sway. Much of the country’s influence depends on whether foreign partners believe that the deals it strikes today will be implemented tomorrow. That credibility, in turn, rests on the state’s capacity to commit—that is, its ability to mobilize the resources needed to fulfill its promises, coordinate public institutions effectively, and ensure that the bargains it makes survive democratic political turnover. A raft of domestic problems, including mounting fiscal constraints, a political system at war with itself, and widespread corruption, has made it harder for the state to deliver. A major scandal has now engulfed the Supreme Court, an institution meant to enforce rules impartially and which is therefore essential to the durability of Brazilian commitments. The Trump administration’s open meddling in Brazil’s domestic politics has compounded the country’s vulnerabilities by making any deal controversial and partisan and raising the likelihood that future administrations in both Brasília and Washington might try to reverse it.
Whoever wins the upcoming presidential election will inherit these sources of weakness. So far, the candidates have not offered any clear plan to address them. Neither a tilt toward Washington nor an embrace of multilateral diplomacy will solve the deeper problem that is eroding Brazil’s foreign policy autonomy and keeping it from turning its assets into real strength.
Brazil has not always struggled to project credibility to the world. In the 1990s, the country’s economic stabilization plan brought down runaway inflation, its leaders consolidated and strengthened its democracy, and it signed agreements with Argentina on economic integration and nuclear safeguards that improved regional security. All these commitments persisted through multiple leadership transitions. In the eyes of powerful players such as Europe and the United States, Brazil was an appealing place for investment and a growing force in multilateral diplomacy.
Today, however, what partners see is a country beset by dire fiscal problems, deeply fragmented domestic politics, and endemic corruption. Brazil’s economy is roughly the size of Canada’s and larger than Spain’s, and the government has a formidable capacity to tax its citizens and bring in revenue. But more than 90 percent of the federal government’s noninterest spending is mandatory, giving it little room for discretionary spending on areas such as infrastructure, which the country sorely needs to make use of its vast reserves of critical minerals. At the same time, the International Monetary Fund has projected that Brazil’s government debt will reach about 98 percent of GDP by the end of 2026. With real interest rates at about ten percent, servicing that debt is extraordinarily expensive, consuming resources that might otherwise be used to strengthen the country’s security forces or fund other strategic priorities.
The country’s fiscal constraints are making it harder to curb the transnational expansion of homegrown criminal gangs, a failure that forces other countries to manage Brazilian problems and further undermines the country’s credibility as a partner. Brazilian authorities do not have enough money to keep up with the vast criminal networks that operate over 1,500 clandestine airstrips across the Amazon River basin; illegally transport drugs, gold, weapons, and other goods across borders between Brazil and its ten neighbors; and exploit a permeable, nearly 5,000-mile coastline. As Brazil’s finances tighten, the threat is evolving far faster than the Brazilian state can direct resources to combat it.
Brazil is also struggling to make government agencies work together. These agencies are staffed by highly professional officials who must pass exams to serve; the agencies themselves, however, compete for authority and resources, which means they viciously fight and undercut each other. Responsibility for security policy, for instance, is fragmented among federal police, highway police, an intelligence agency, individual military and civilian police forces in all 26 states and the federal district (which contains the capital city of Brasília), the armed forces, a federal revenue department, and independent federal and state prosecutors. Attempts to coordinate the different agencies under a central authority to fight organized crime have failed in Congress, where professional associations representing those agencies have resisted anything that would reduce their power. As a result, no single authority can set priorities or quickly mobilize resources, and criminal organizations have proliferated in the bureaucracy’s seams.
Brazil’s internal fragmentation hinders international cooperation, too. Different agencies claim overlapping authority and do not coordinate when pursuing their priorities, making it difficult for the state to act as a unified entity. Even with neighboring countries such as Paraguay and Uruguay, where Brazilian criminal networks have proliferated but which lack the resources to fight them alone, Brazil has not found ways to build sustained mechanisms for intelligence sharing, joint operations, and coordinated enforcement.
As Brazil has lost the ability to control its own security agenda, decisions about how to handle criminal gangs operating from its territory are increasingly made outside the country. The Trump administration has designated the Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho, Brazil’s two most prominent criminal organizations, as terrorist groups, granting the United States new financial and legal tools to fight them. Several governments in Latin America have joined Washington in its anticartel policy. As a result, Brazil is becoming the object of other countries’ security policies rather than the author of its own.
Although corruption has long dogged some of Brazil’s most ambitious foreign policy projects, recent public scandals have dealt a blow to the country’s reputation. Major scandals involving Petrobras, the state oil company, and construction giants financed by the national development bank BNDES upended large deals that Brazil had secured across Latin America. These scandals, which included massive bribes and kickbacks on projects across the continent, contributed to a political crisis that, in 2016, ended Dilma Rousseff’s presidency and, in 2018, sent Lula to prison. (His convictions were later annulled.) Later in 2018, the scandals fueled the anti-establishment backlash that carried Jair Bolsonaro to power. Judges and prosecutors who had uncovered and investigated the corruption emerged from that period with extraordinary political authority, presenting themselves as a check on a political class that had failed the Brazilian people.
Starting in late 2025, however, the public began to learn how deeply parts of the judiciary had become entangled in corruption. The owner of Banco Master, a bank that offered above-market interest rates, is alleged to have given side payments and lucrative contracts to families of Supreme Court justices and loaned his private jets to justices for personal travel. A court whose authority rested in part on its ability to stand up to elected governments is now under suspicion, raising doubts as to whether it can hold the next administration to account.
The scandal has overtaken the upcoming election and raised the stakes of its outcome. Flávio Bolsonaro is himself under investigation over alleged links to Banco Master; he has promised to confront the court that convicted his father, including by pardoning him. Lula has not been directly implicated in the scandal, but figures close to his government have been drawn into the investigation. Whoever wins the election will also be able to appoint at least three of the court’s 11 justices, effectively granting him the power to reshape the institution.
Corruption has an outsize effect on Brazil’s foreign policy. The country’s scandals have repeatedly brought down the companies and institutions that were able to project Brazil’s influence abroad. At the beginning of the twenty-first century, Petrobras and large construction firms were building Brazil’s regional clout through development; the scandals of the 2010s undercut their influence. Today, it is the courts, meant to ensure that rules remain above politics, that are losing authority. Partners cannot tell which agreements will be ensnared in the next scandal, which encourages them to hedge. Governments and firms considering large, long-term investments in Brazil in areas such as critical minerals, energy, agriculture, or infrastructure are likely to pursue stronger investment guarantees, demand greater control over deal terms, or simply pursue less ambitious arrangements with lower risk.
For decades, Brazil increased the credibility of its commitments by tying its hands internationally. Adherence to World Trade Organization rules, for example, made it harder for protectionist politicians at home to oppose trade openness, and signing on to human rights treaties helped constrain domestic security forces that wanted to continue practices such as torture and extrajudicial violence that they had inherited from the era of military rule. Agreeing to global banking standards strengthened the Brazilian central bank’s ability to impose tough rules on the financial system. These external constraints gave Brazilian leaders the leverage to overcome domestic opposition, and they also gave Brazil’s foreign partners greater confidence in the country. Now, with global rules under heavy attack, there are fewer bulwarks against domestic interests seeking privileged access to public contracts, regulatory favors, or political protection.
The Trump administration has made the problem far worse. Washington’s attempt to influence domestic politics in Brazil has raised the cost to Brasília of going against U.S. preferences. If the United States can force Brazil to undo its previous promises, Brazil’s standing in Washington might go up but its credibility would plummet with every other partner. It cuts the other way, too: if U.S.-Brazilian relations depend on arrangements that the White House makes contingent on political results or ties to personal relationships, future U.S. administrations will have more reason to dismiss them as partisan and may try to undo or change them.
Meanwhile, competition among great powers has become more zero-sum, putting every one of Brazil’s partnerships under constant scrutiny. Whether Brazil is deciding which country should supply its 5G telecom networks or which country’s technology should underpin its emerging AI infrastructure, its partners must believe that Brasília will honor its commitments even when a rival power pressures it to back away. The weaker Brazil’s credibility, the less room it has to sustain close ties with multiple competing powers.
In the battle over critical minerals, Brazil dominates global production of niobium, a metal used in high-strength steel production, and has major reserves of rare earths, but China dominates rare-earth processing. The United States, worried by this dominance, is trying to push supply chains away from Chinese-controlled companies. Producers are already being squeezed between competing supply chains. Viridis Mining & Minerals, an Australian company developing the Colossus rare-earth project in the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais, has said it plans to sell only to U.S. and European buyers despite Chinese interest. Yet China buys nearly 30 percent of Brazil’s total exports and has become a major investor in electricity, mining, automobiles, oil, and other strategic sectors. Brazil needs to be able to reassure multiple sides, but doing so is increasingly difficult when both the United States and China, for example, think Brasília might cave to pressure from the other.
A lack of credibility may also drive potential partners away. Brazil experienced this situation before when, after discovering offshore oil deposits, it rewrote the rules governing its most valuable oil fields to empower the federal government. When it auctioned the rights to develop the enormous Libra oil field, in 2013, only one consortium made a viable bid—and it offered the minimum allowed under the revised terms. Brazil thought it would make more money from its newly valuable assets, but abruptly changing the rules of the game cost the country the power to set the terms of a new deal.
Countries like Brazil have multiple ways to make their commitments credible. In Gulf Arab states, for example, the solution to a credibility gap is concentrated authority. Foreign counterparts have confidence that Gulf countries will implement their side of any bargain because political power is centralized enough for leaders to ensure that state bureaucracies follow through. Strong democracies, by contrast, rely on impersonal institutions that protect state promises from day-to-day political interference and on budgets large enough for these institutions to carry them out.
Brazil has neither the concentrated authority of an autocracy nor democratic institutions strong enough to serve the same function. It struggles to make credible state guarantees, and its fiscal position limits the resources to uphold them.
The two presidential candidates offer different solutions for restoring credibility. Flávio Bolsonaro wants to borrow credibility from Washington through closer alignment with the United States, including greater openness to U.S. critical minerals plans that call for keeping supply chains outside Chinese control. That may reassure the Trump administration, but it would alarm Beijing and put Brazil at the mercy of a single patron whose foreign policy is highly transactional. Agreeing to terms that squeeze out China or others might make it possible to sign more deals with the United States, but it would come with an even higher cost—making Brazil less credible as an independent partner to other major powers.
Lula proposes preserving Brazil’s autonomy by simultaneously strengthening ties with all major powers and engaging in multilateral diplomacy as much as possible. This would ensure that the country is not solely reliant on Washington, but it puts an even greater strain on Brazil’s already overstretched institutions by multiplying the relationships Brazil must sustain and invest in. The strategy works only if different partners believe that Brazil can honor several commitments at once, even when forces pull it in different directions.
Neither strategy does much to restore Brazil’s credibility because neither rebuilds the capacity on which that credibility rests. Brazil may still find some ways to work with partners abroad, but it will only be able to do so at higher cost. This creates a vicious cycle in which each new arrangement leaves Brazil with less room to maneuver and makes subsequent deals even more difficult. This cycle is taking hold just as Brazilian resources, exports, and investments are becoming more valuable to the rest of the world, which is the moment when the country’s leverage should be growing rather than declining.
The vote that begins on October 4—and the likely runoff three weeks later between the top two vote getters—will not break this cycle on its own. Doing so requires a long-term effort to ensure that Brazil has the funding, cohesion, and trustworthy institutions needed to make ambitious agreements and get them to stick. What voters will decide instead is how Brazil manages its credibility deficit and whether the country can start the long process of closing it.
articles.summary: Reckoning with the country’s real crisis.

articles.title: Palestinians Want a Two-State Solution
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
MICHAEL ROBBINS is Director and Co-Principal Investigator at Arab Barometer.
AMANEY A. JAMAL is Co-Founder and Co-Principal Investigator at Arab Barometer, Dean of the Princeton School of Public and International Affairs, and Edwards S. Sanford Professor of Politics and International Affairs at Princeton University.
MARK TESSLER is Co-Founder and Co-Principal Investigator at Arab Barometer and Samuel J. Eldersveld Professor of Politics at the University of Michigan.
In September 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump unveiled a peace plan to end the war in Gaza, vowing it would not only rebuild the devastated territory but also usher in “eternal peace in the Middle East.” A year later, the plan has stalled. Hamas has not disarmed. Israel still controls more than 60 percent of the strip. A promised technocratic government and international security force has not materialized, and large-scale reconstruction has barely begun; most Gazans still struggle to obtain food, water, and shelter. And as Israel’s October election approaches, the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has hardened his position, rejecting a U.S.-backed disarmament deal. Although the 25-country Board of Peace—the mechanism Trump established to implement his peace plan—did announce a more detailed reconstruction program this week, high-level officials have told the Times of Israel and other outlets that the group has stopped pressuring Netanyahu to comply with the plan because of the upcoming vote.
This hard-line stance appeals to the majority of Israelis, who do not think that Palestinians are interested in negotiations or diplomacy. Surveys have repeatedly shown that Israelis overwhelmingly believe Palestinians do not want peace at all and, therefore, that Israel has no real negotiating partner. In July of this year, for instance, a Tel Aviv University poll asked Jewish Israelis what they think Palestinians want. Seventy-two percent said they believed Palestinians were “moderately or very opposed” to any peace negotiations, and over 80 percent said they believed Palestinians thought no peace with Israel was achievable.
But this perception completely distorts what most Palestinians believe and are prepared to accept. For two decades, Arab Barometer, a survey project that we help run, has carried out comprehensive polls of Palestinian public opinion in both the West Bank and Gaza. Our most recent broad survey, conducted in October 2025, showed that a majority of Palestinians regard diplomatic negotiations, not armed resistance, as the best way to resolve the Israeli-Palestinian conflict for good; conditions on the ground have not changed in a way that would meaningfully modify these findings, and they are backed up by questions asked this August by the Ramallah-based Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research (PCPSR), an Arab Barometer partner.
In fact, many Palestinians have a clear and realistic vision for the future. Far more of them support a two-state option than any other potential resolution. And Gazans, despite having borne the brunt of destruction over the past three years, tend to be the most pragmatic: an even greater proportion of them are open to a two-state solution than are Palestinians living in the West Bank, and half of Gazans would back Arab states’ normalization of diplomatic ties with Israel as long as the process includes tangible progress toward Palestinian self-determination. Palestinians’ confidence in both Hamas and the Palestinian Authority (PA) has also deeply eroded; they judge that neither faction has secured their safety or improved their lives, and they want political renewal. Strikingly, most Gazans express a wish to stay and help rebuild their devastated homeland rather than emigrate.
Gaza’s immediate situation is bleak. The conditions for Palestinians living in the West Bank are deteriorating rapidly. The status quo is not sustainable, despite there being no clear end to conflict in sight. But Palestinians’ own views offer glimmers of hope. Israelis have a chance to choose a new government more committed to negotiation. If such a government and international donors were to pursue a transition that treats Palestinian statehood as a central part of negotiations and recognizes Gazans’ desire for security and legitimate governance, Gazans are ready to compromise, as are many Palestinians in the West Bank. They are willing to work toward a new political order, but it must be just that: new.
Last October’s Arab Barometer survey revealed just how desperate conditions had become in both Gaza and the West Bank—a security, economic, and humanitarian crisis that has not improved meaningfully since then. The survey polled 855 people in Gaza face-to-face in the respondents’ homes, shelters, or camps, and 800 in the West Bank face-to-face in the respondents’ homes. It began the same day that a formal cease-fire in Gaza was announced, providing a broad picture of the conditions confronting the strip’s rebuilding. Because of the survey’s timing, some questions that were asked in the West Bank and other countries across the Middle East (such as queries about domestic politics and social relations) were not asked in Gaza to make room for questions that would bring to light Gazans’ immediate needs. Since the 2025 Arab Barometer poll, no similar survey has been done to capture Gaza’s humanitarian situation; given the limited aid that has been allowed to enter Gaza and the Board of Peace’s failure to make real progress past the cease-fire’s first phase, the scale of the challenge remains largely unchanged.
In our survey, 85 percent of Gazans indicated that they had been displaced at least once since early October 2023. Among those who had been displaced, 70 percent had been uprooted three or more times. Sixty-one percent of Gazans said that a member of their household had lost employment as a result of the war, and under half said they had eaten every day in the past week. Just over one in five had gone all or most of the past seven days without eating. Education had also been badly disrupted: among households with school-age children, 31 percent said none of their children currently had access to education. Other essential services remained limited. Only nine percent of Gazans had access to electricity and six percent to fuel or cooking gas, crises that have persisted. In early September, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs reported that Gaza still had a “near-total absence of reliable electricity,” while prior reports noted that Gazans had to burn trash to cook.
Residents of the West Bank had more access to basic services but reported rapidly deteriorating security. Only 58 percent of Palestinians in the West Bank described their neighborhood as safe, a 16-point decline from the poll completed in October 2023. Two-thirds rated the PA’s provision of security as “bad” or “very bad,” and 24 percent had considered emigrating. We asked those who wanted to leave the West Bank to tell us why, in their own words. Overall, 38 percent included security reasons in their answers, 37 percent included political reasons, and 71 percent included economic reasons. This contrasts with most other countries we survey, where few would-be emigrants cite major motives other than economic ones.
The West Bank’s economic crisis is becoming more deeply felt. Fully 92 percent of respondents described the area’s economic condition as “bad” or “very bad,” an increase of 21 points from two years prior. Hunger is also a major problem. Fifty-one percent of West Bank Palestinians agreed that the statement “the food that we bought did not last and we did not have money to get more” was often or sometimes true over the past 30 days. And 41 percent agreed that they “had to skip a meal” for lack of money or resources over the course of the previous 12 months.
And yet Gazans, in particular, had not become fatalistic. A majority of Gazans told Arab Barometer surveyors that neither they nor their household would “leave Gaza right now if they could.” The percentage of those who said that they, or both they and their household, would leave the strip now if they could—41 percent—resembled the percentage of those who have considered emigrating from other, vastly more peaceful and stable societies (such as Jordan, 44 percent, and Tunisia, 41 percent) in surveys conducted in the fall of 2025 by Arab Barometer. In other words, despite living in horrific circumstances, most Gazans want to remain and rebuild.
One might also assume that, given the scale of devastation in Gaza and settler violence in the West Bank, support for a negotiated settlement to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict might have declined. This was not the case. When respondents in the West Bank were asked which solution they preferred to end the Israeli-Palestinian conflict—two states, one state, a confederation, or “other”—56 percent selected a two-state solution, a rise of seven points from the Arab Barometer survey conducted in 2023. Over the course of two years of devastating conflict, support for a two-state solution had risen even more in Gaza, from 54 percent in early October of 2023 to 64 percent in October 2025. Over the same time frame, support for a confederation increased by ten points in Gaza, to 20 percent; support for one state dropped by four points, to five percent; and support for “other”—a choice that often reflects a preference for armed resistance—fell from 20 percent to seven percent in Gaza.
Notably, the rise in support for a two-state solution was especially large among younger Palestinians. In 2023, Palestinians between the ages of 18 and 29 were nine points less likely to favor the two-state solution than those 30 or older. By the fall of 2025, they were no less likely than those 30 and older to favor this outcome. Meanwhile, among young Palestinians, support for the “other” option had been cut in half by 2025, falling from 27 percent to 14 percent.
Newer polling confirms these views remain solid. A 440-person sample of Gazans conducted by the PCPSR in early August this year found that 61 percent preferred a two-state solution based on 1967 borders over other options such as a single equal state. Sixty-five percent of Gazans agreed that armed resistance had failed to protect Palestinians and had instead brought destruction.
Gazans exhibit particular pragmatism. In Arab Barometer’s October 2025 survey, when respondents in both occupied Palestinian territories were asked whether they supported Arab countries normalizing diplomatic ties with Israel, only 11 percent did. But substantially more Gazans supported such an outcome than did Palestinians living in the West Bank—nearly one in five. In contrast, in Arab Barometer’s October 2023 survey, just ten percent of Gazans favored normalization and five percent of Palestinians living in the West Bank did. In 2025, when respondents were asked whether they supported Arab-Israeli normalization if it were linked to the creation of a Palestinian state (a condition Saudi Arabia, in particular, has recently insisted on), fully half of Gazans and more than a quarter of West Bank Palestinians said yes.
The data was clear: more Gazans support a peace process than favor violent confrontation. The survey results also challenged a widespread misconception. A majority of Gazans prioritize securing independence over seeking revenge on Israel. A key reason Palestinians oppose normalization is the possibility that it proceeds without Palestinian independence. When independence is added, support for the concept increases dramatically.
Palestinians are also firm in their belief that their existing leaders have failed them. For decades, Palestinian politics have revolved around two key factions: Fatah, the party that controls the PA, and Hamas. Analysts have often assumed a decline in support for one translates into gains for the other. A reformed PA would be better than the status quo, but it is clear that a fuller reform of the Palestinian political system is needed. By now, most Palestinians do not support either Hamas or the PA. In the October 2025 Arab Barometer survey, when Palestinians living in the West Bank were asked which political party they felt closest to, 24 percent indicated Hamas and 18 percent indicated Fatah; 51 percent indicated no party, “don’t know,” or refused to provide a response. Just 23 percent said they had confidence in the PA’s governance, barely an improvement from 2023’s 19 percent. Trust in the PA’s president, Mahmoud Abbas, was even lower, at just 19 percent.
In our 2023 survey, only 29 percent of Gazans expressed confidence in their Hamas-led government; 72 percent criticized substantial corruption in government institutions. Although the survey included fewer questions on Palestinians’ broad political outlook in Gaza than it did in the West Bank (to make room for more questions about Gazans’ immediate needs), it was clear that Hamas’s horrific October 7 attack on Israel and the subsequent war did not win it any support in the long run. In the October 2025 survey, roughly the same percentage of Gazans—only a third—expressed confidence in what remains of the territory’s Hamas-led government.
Palestinians simply do not want either Hamas or Fatah to lead them. When they were asked whom they would choose in a hypothetical legislative election featuring the same parties that ran in 2006, 16 percent of Palestinians across both territories selected Fatah, and 19 percent said they would support Hamas’s Change and Reform list. A total of 55 percent said they would either not support any party that had stood in the 2006 elections or not vote at all. The largest bloc in Palestinian politics is not Fatah or Hamas; it is the politically alienated. The August PCPSR survey showed that nearly 40 percent of Palestinians prefer Marwan Barghouti—a leader of the first Palestinian intifada who has been imprisoned in Israel since 2002 and was convicted of murder in 2004—as their presidential candidate, more than double the support garnered by any other figure. But Israel has repeatedly refused to free him in prisoner exchanges, and recent reports suggest that he is in very poor health.
Returning the PA to Gaza, even after a reform process, will not yield a legitimate government. Palestinians do not believe the PA can effectively provide security: majorities of Palestinians in the West Bank distrust both the PA-led National Security Forces, the territory’s closest organization it has to an army, and the PA’s police. (Neither of these organizations operated in Gaza at the time of the survey and still do not.)
One potential path forward would be to create a technocratic government to oversee the transition in Gaza. There is some support among Palestinians for such a concept: according to the August 2026 PCPSR survey, 43 percent in Gaza would prefer the National Committee proposed by the Board of Peace to oversee Gaza in the near term, while 34 percent would favor elections to form a government. (In the West Bank, support for both options is lower, at 24 percent for each.) Although a technocratic government may be a necessary first step to stabilize Gaza and allow for more humanitarian assistance and reconstruction, entrenching such a government in the long term risks further institutionalizing the separation of Gaza from the West Bank. As Salam Fayyad, the Palestinian prime minister from 2007 to 2013, noted in a recent interview with Foreign Affairs, a unified and nonfactional transitional government for both areas is essential.
Although the percentage of West Bank Palestinians who agreed that democracy is the “best system” of governance remained effectively unchanged between our 2023 (78 percent) and 2025 surveys (77 percent), support for a strong leader who “bends the rules if necessary to get things done” rose by ten points during this period, from 41 percent to 51 percent. Two-thirds of respondents agreed that “as long as a government can solve our country’s economic problems, it does not matter what kind of government we have.” Given the destruction in Gaza and the ongoing security crises in the West Bank, Palestinians clearly strongly desire a leader capable of bringing order and stability. But this does not mean that Palestinians do not favor democracy. It is better understood as a symptom of political exhaustion and vulnerability following years of division, economic hardship, and war. Palestinians prefer democracy, but ultimately they want results from their political system.
Palestinians’ own views offer clear directions for efforts to end the Gaza conflict and reconstruct the territory. And any discussion of rebuilding needs to reflect their preferences. After all, although Palestinians’ loss of faith in the PA has a great deal to do with the organization’s corruption, it also reflects the fact that the PA often prioritized meeting Israelis’ security demands even as the expansion of settlements into the West Bank contributed to its delegitimization. The growing impression that the PA functioned as an arm of the Israeli occupation and not a vehicle for authentic Palestinian political representation and expression directly fueled Hamas’s rise in popularity in the middle of the first decade of this century. Such a grave mistake must not be made again.
Simply inserting the PA into Gaza without a plan to address its legitimacy deficit cannot lead to stability. Any proposal premised on a large number of Gazans leaving the territory before reconstruction begins, such as a September 2026 plan unveiled by Israel’s national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, will also be misguided. Gazans want to stay and transform their homeland on their own terms and live side by side with the state of Israel.
More broadly, surveys show that even as Palestinians have withdrawn from their two main political factions, they have not lost interest in policy or policy outcomes. They have a clear vision and are willing to back compromise. But despite their exhaustion, they will not accept any result that simply ends the fighting and keeps their future in limbo.
Gaza’s future cannot be divorced from the West Bank’s. Stabilizing the strip will be challenging enough in a vacuum, and it will be immensely harder while settlements and settler violence expand in the West Bank. Palestinians are also clear that any near-term solution must include a credible route to independent statehood; a Palestinian state must not be treated as a possible reward at the end of a long and uncertain path. Palestinians are far more likely to be willing to respect Israel’s role in the region—as represented by its normalization of ties with other Arab states—when they, too, are allowed self-determination. The question of Palestinian statehood cannot be left for the end of a peace process, and the prospect of it must be credible to ensure Palestinians’ engagement with political renewal.
Palestinians, particularly those in Gaza, have been deeply traumatized. Frustration runs deep, and rebuilding will take years, if not decades. But the Arab Barometer’s findings staunchly contradict any view of Palestinian politics as rigidly ideological, committed to revenge, and supportive of violence. On the contrary, Palestinians are notably pragmatic—especially in Gaza, where one might expect radicalization. They have not rejected the idea of a peaceful settlement with Israel. Despite their disillusionment with the PA, they are not turning toward Hamas or toward violent resistance. Although there is Palestinian opposition to a two-state solution, a growing proportion—now a majority—wants it, and yearns for more capable and responsible leadership that addresses their needs and provides security.
articles.summary: A new majority—even in Gaza—support compromise with Israel.
